$comment: Humanist Minimal type direction. Fonts come from foundations/typography/source/pairings.json; this file says which suit this approach and how to set them. Sizes are rules of thumb unless a source is given.
character: Humanist letterforms (from the broad-nib pen: open apertures, slight stroke variation, varied proportions) set with modern restraint (few sizes, sentence case, generous space). The type is calm and clear so the hand-drawn art can carry the warmth.

anatomy.$comment: What to look for when judging a typeface for this approach.

apertures.why: Open c, e, a, s stay distinct at small sizes and at a distance; a humanist trait (Frutiger was drawn for airport signage).

strokes.why: Matches the even ink line; strong contrast feels formal rather than human.

terminals.why: Echo the rounded corners and organic shapes.

proportions.why: Letters of different widths read as written, not engineered.

xHeight.why: Readable on phones and at poster distance.

italic.why: Italics carry the hand; use for one emphasised word.

avoid: Handwriting fonts for headlines or body (the hand lives in the art; one short note is allowed)
Geometric fonts with closed apertures at small sizes

fit.$comment: core = recommended, good = works, accent = special cases, avoid = not for this approach.

bricolage-figtree.why: Slightly irregular display forms echo the hand-drawn line; Figtree is open and calm.

young-onest.why: Soft, heavy serif with rounded details; matches organic shapes and warmth.

source.why: A true humanist superfamily; the most readable choice for text-heavy work.

instrument.why: Editorial and calm; the condensed serif leaves room for big illustrations.

nunito.why: Rounded terminals mirror rounded corners; keep headlines bold and the body plain so it stays grown-up.

alegreya.why: Calligraphic and literary: the most 'hand' in the type. Use where storytelling matters.

fraunces-commissioner.why: Soft serif charm; restrain to one weight to avoid novelty.

schibsted.why: Very minimal; works when the illustration carries all the warmth.

plex.why: Engineered feel; for data-heavy or technical products only.

handwritten.$comment: Handwritten accent faces from foundations/typography/source/handwritten.json. use: none | accent (one short element) | core (part of the style). A product picks one in brand.json -> typography.hand.
handwritten.why: The hand mainly lives in the ink line. One short note in a plain pen hand can add a person to warm pieces (Schroll et al. 2018), as long as the headline and body stay in the pairing.

typeWithArt.weightMatch: Headline stem thickness should be close to the ink line width (about 2.25% of the artboard's short side at headline size). Pick the headline weight that gets closest.
typeWithArt.scaleMatch: Headline cap height between 1/3 and 2/3 of the motif's height, so neither dominates by accident.
typeWithArt.alignment: Align text to one edge of the grid; let the motif be the only free-form element.
typeWithArt.spacing: At least one margin between text and the motif.

sizes.$comment: Headline cap height as a share of the canvas height, and body text minimums. Rules of thumb.
sizes.viewingDistance: Sign-industry rule of thumb: about 1 inch (25 mm) of letter height for every 10 feet (3 m) of viewing distance for basic legibility; double it for comfortable reading.

measure.source: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style

setting.case: Sentence case everywhere. Capitals only for labels of one to three words.
setting.rag: Ragged right; no justified text; avoid single words on the last line of headlines (use text-wrap: balance).
setting.numbers: Use the mono for dates, times, prices and codes (tabular figures).

rules: Three sizes and two weights per piece.
Headline weight matches the ink line.
Left-aligned, sentence case, 45-75 characters per line.
At most one short handwritten note (six words or fewer) in a listed hand face; never the headline, body or call to action.
